CausalChain: Tumor cells release EVs enriched in specific lipids and miRNAs -> EV uptake by mature myeloid cells leads to downregulation of the transcription factor IRF8 -> Impaired IRF8 activity prevents normal differentiation into mature, immunogenic myeloid cells -> Myeloid cells are reprogrammed into immunosuppressive MDSCs -> Accumulation of MDSCs in the tumor microenvironment promotes immune evasion and tumor progression
Hypothesis: Specific lipid components within tumor-derived extracellular vesicles drive the downregulation of IRF8 in mature myeloid cells, thereby converting them into MDSCs; targeting these EV-associated lipids could reverse this conversion, restore effective myeloid cell differentiation, and enhance the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy.
Abstract: Recent studies have revealed that tumor‐released extracellular vesicles (EVs) play a pivotal role in subverting myeloid cell differentiation and fueling the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Building on evidence that EVs contain a cargo of proteins, lipids, and miRNAs capable of reprogramming mature myeloid cells toward a suppressive MDSC phenotype via transcriptional regulators such as IRF8, we propose that specific lipid moieties within EVs are key drivers of this process. Our novel hypothesis suggests that these EV-associated lipids downregulate IRF8 in recipient myeloid cells, thereby blocking their normal differentiation into antigen‐presenting cells and compelling their conversion into potent MDSCs. Consequently, the accumulation of such metabolically reprogrammed MDSCs enhances immune evasion and tumor progression. Targeting the lipid components of tumor-derived EVs may disrupt this pathogenic signaling cascade, restore normal myelopoiesis, and improve the efficacy of immunotherapeutic interventions.
